title: Infrastructure-scale wireless electrical power delivery

concept.text: The innovation would deliver useful electrical power across operationally valuable distances without a continuous physical conductor between transmitter and receiver. A complete system would combine an electrical supply, beam formation and control, transmission through the environment, a receiver, and conversion back into electricity for a load. The defining advance would be sustained, dependable service at practical cost, extending beyond a brief demonstration of power transfer or detection of a transmitted signal.

The concept encompasses terrestrial links and potential space-based applications. Space solar power would add orbital generation and space-to-Earth transmission, but neither orbital generation nor any particular energy source is required for wireless delivery itself. Its central engineering work concerns beams, receivers, power electronics and system integration, with additional demands from atmospheric propagation, aerospace operations, safety and infrastructure economics.

significance.text: If continuous delivery became economical and dependable, it could supply locations where installing wires or transporting fuel is unusually difficult, including disaster zones and remote operating sites. The direct benefit would be access to usable energy across otherwise costly logistical gaps. That benefit depends on the complete delivery system, including its receiving equipment and operating conditions, rather than transmission distance alone.

Moving platforms could gain new operating possibilities if receivers could obtain power while moving. DARPA discusses prospective integration with unmanned aerial vehicles, grounding this application in an actual development direction. Sustained mobile service would additionally require reliable tracking, beam control and platform integration; it was not established by the reported ground-to-ground experiment. Space solar power is another conditional downstream possibility, requiring a much larger generation and delivery system than the Caltech experiment demonstrated.

Assessment: access and mobility are especially compelling reasons to pursue this capability because they address situations in which conventional delivery is difficult. This is a judgment about potential value, not an established ranking of applications. Successful wireless links would not by themselves imply economical replacement of conventional grids everywhere: each application would still need to justify conversion losses, equipment, availability and cost against its alternatives.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is an integrated system that sustains useful electrical delivery over a valuable distance under realistic operating conditions. The supplied reports identify pieces of this problem: atmospheric effects during terrestrial propagation, receiver conversion, directed transmission and beam steering, and hardware cost and mass requirements. Combining these pieces must preserve usable output and dependable operation across the entire chain.

Engineering assessment: diffraction and transmitter–receiver aperture trade-offs, weather-dependent losses, tracking accuracy, beam containment, exposure, interference and full-system economics remain necessary assessment topics. Their acceptable limits would depend on wavelength, geometry, environment and application. The supplied evidence does not quantify all these constraints or establish their present-day severity. That incomplete characterization leaves questions open; it does not show that the constraints are absent or that practical delivery is impossible.

Efficiency is a system boundary problem as well as a component problem. A receiver can convert a useful fraction of incident beam power while the complete installation loses additional energy in producing the beam and delivering it to that receiver. Demonstrating infrastructure viability therefore requires electrical-input-to-useful-electrical-output measurements alongside component efficiencies. DARPA’s separately reported optical-to-electrical efficiency does not resolve that full-system requirement.

current_state.text: DARPA’s May 16, 2025 institutional report states that an optical power-beaming demonstration delivered more than 800 W over 8.6 km during a 30-second transmission. This establishes a reported combination of useful received power, kilometer-scale distance and short duration. It does not establish continuous infrastructure service, competitive economics or performance across a representative range of operating conditions.

The same report separately gives greater than 20% efficiency from laser optical output to receiver electrical output at shorter distances. That value is not a reported efficiency for the 8.6 km result, and it excludes the electrical energy required to generate the laser output. It must therefore not be presented as wall-plug efficiency or combined with the longest-distance result as though both were measured under the same conditions.

Caltech’s June 1, 2023 report describes its MAPLE experiment transferring power wirelessly to two receiver arrays about a foot away aboard its space demonstrator. The receivers converted the received energy to direct current and powered LEDs. Separately, Caltech reported detecting a transmission from orbit on an Earth-based rooftop receiver on May 22, identifying it through timing, frequency and Doppler shift. Nearby electrical delivery in space and detection on Earth are distinct achievements; the Earth detection does not establish useful Earth-delivered electrical power.

These are dated institutional reports of demonstrations, rather than independent validation of infrastructure-scale operation. The supplied review describes complete, untruncated saved HTML texts for both reports, so the earlier DARPA retrieval timeout no longer limits interpretation of the reported figures. However, the supplied materials contain no bounded freshness search establishing the frontier or continued openness of the capability as of November 1, 2026. Development goals and prospective applications in these reports should remain distinct from demonstrated service.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: independently verify sustained delivery of substantial useful electrical power over a distance and under conditions where wiring or fuel delivery is genuinely difficult. Before testing, define application-specific requirements for useful output, distance, duration, availability, permissible interruptions, exposure and interference. These would be proposed acceptance criteria for the intended service, not established universal standards.
completion_criteria.label: Independently verify sustained substantial power against predefined service requirements

completion_criteria.text: Proposed measurements: report electrical input to the complete transmitting installation and useful electrical output at the receiving load, with clearly defined boundaries and measurement uncertainty. Record component efficiencies separately, together with weather availability, pointing and tracking performance, beam containment, safety behavior, capital cost and maintenance. A mobile application should demonstrate these outcomes during representative motion rather than infer them from a stationary link.
completion_criteria.label: Report full-system power accounting, operational performance and costs

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: enable independent replication or verification and demonstrate operation at several sites against appropriate wired or fuel-delivery alternatives. Compare full-system costs for equivalent service, including required supporting equipment and downtime. Several sites would provide evidence of breadth, not literal universality; an infrastructure-scale claim should specify the power, distance, climate, mobility and operating conditions for which performance has actually been demonstrated.
completion_criteria.label: Multisite verification reports comparative service costs and demonstrated operating limits

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: ELE-01, Practical ambient-temperature superconducting conductors, concerns improved conductive delivery, while ELE-07 concerns crossing a gap by wireless transmission. Both could affect power infrastructure, but success in either would not establish the other. ELE-05, Cheap, scalable storage for weeks to seasons of electrical supply, addresses when energy is available; storage could complement a wireless link during interruptions, while transmission alone does not provide long-duration reserves.

Roster-based synthesis: ELE-09, Resilient, self-restoring power networks, overlaps in dependable service and recovery from disruptions. A wireless link could be a network component, but resilience requires broader coordination and restoration capabilities. ELE-10, Broadly deployable, maintenance-free ambient-powered sensing, also concerns powering devices without routine wired supply or battery maintenance. Its defining source is ambient energy, whereas deliberate delivery from a transmitter belongs to a different system architecture.

Roster-based synthesis: ELE-11, Integrated photonic-electronic computing with broad system advantage, shares optical and electronic conversion themes with optical power beaming, but concerns computation rather than remote energy delivery. ELE-03, A long-distance quantum repeater network, also involves transmission infrastructure, but its purpose is quantum communication; demonstrating an energy-carrying beam does not demonstrate quantum repeaters.

Roster-based synthesis: ELE-02, Fault-tolerant quantum computer with useful, scalable logical computation; ELE-04, Practical, energy-recovering reversible computing; and ELE-08, Manufacturable ultra-low-voltage switching for general-purpose electronics, address computation or its energy requirements rather than delivery across distance. ELE-06, Durable, high-bandwidth two-way neural interface, addresses a biological communication interface. These remain distinct innovations even where future systems might use wireless power as an enabling component.

unresolved_issues: The supplied materials do not establish subsequent progress or whether infrastructure-scale operation remained unachieved as of November 1, 2026.
Full electrical-input-to-useful-output efficiency for the 8.6 km DARPA demonstration is not supplied; the shorter-distance optical-to-electrical figure cannot substitute for it.
Sustained operation, representative weather availability, mobile tracking performance and competitive full-system economics are not established by the reported demonstrations.
Quantitative exposure, interference, diffraction and aperture constraints require application-specific characterization beyond the supplied evidence.
Useful power, distance, duration, availability and economic comparators must be defined for a particular service before the proposed completion criteria can be applied.

brief.title: Dependable electricity delivery without wires
possible: A remote work site or disaster zone could receive steady electricity without a power line or regular fuel deliveries. A transmitter would send energy in a directed beam, and receiving equipment would turn it back into electricity.
Aircraft without pilots could receive power while moving. A larger system could also collect solar energy in orbit and send it to receivers on Earth.
why: For people working where wires are hard to install and fuel is hard to transport, wireless delivery could bridge a costly supply gap. Power could reach places that conventional delivery struggles to serve.
Receiving power on the move could give aircraft new operating possibilities by reducing their dependence on carried fuel.

sources.who: Ali Hajimiri and the Caltech team
sources.showed: The team transferred energy between nearby devices in space and converted it into electricity to light small lamps. Separately, a rooftop receiver on Earth detected a transmission from orbit.
sources.quote: MAPLE tested this in space by lighting up each LED individually and shifting back and forth between them.
sources.cited_for: The experiment demonstrated local electrical delivery in space and a separately detected transmission to Earth.
sources.not_established: Detecting the transmission on Earth did not establish useful electrical power delivered from orbit.

sources.who: DARPA-led team, with receiver design by Teravec Technologies and collaborators
sources.showed: The team briefly delivered useful electrical power over a long ground-to-ground laser link. It separately measured conversion efficiency at shorter distances.
sources.quote: While efficiency wasn’t the focus of this demonstration, the team measured more than 20% efficiency from the optical power out of the laser to the electrical power out of the receiver at shorter distances.
sources.cited_for: The tests support useful power delivery over distance and a separate measurement of beam-to-electricity conversion.
sources.not_established: The tests did not establish sustained service, competitive cost or efficiency including the electricity used to produce the laser beam.

shown: DARPA reported useful electrical power delivered across 8.6 kilometres in a brief ground test. Caltech powered small lights across a short gap in space and separately detected a transmission on Earth. These demonstrations did not establish dependable electricity service.
missing: Sustained useful delivery over a valuable distance under realistic weather and operating conditions has yet to be demonstrated.
Complete measurements must connect electricity entering the transmitter to useful electricity reaching the load.
Moving receivers still need demonstrated tracking, safe beam control and dependable power during representative motion.
Independent tests across several sites must establish service costs and operating limits against wired or fuel-based alternatives.

milestones.label: Independent confirmation of sustained useful power
milestones.explanation: Independent testing would have to confirm sustained delivery against predefined requirements for a hard-to-supply location. This would establish whether the link provides the intended service.

milestones.label: Complete energy, operating and cost measurements
milestones.explanation: Tests would have to measure total electrical input, useful output, weather performance, beam control, safety and costs, including motion where relevant. These measurements would reveal how the complete service performs.

milestones.label: Several sites confirm costs and operating limits
milestones.explanation: Independent checks at several sites would have to compare equivalent service with wires or fuel delivery and identify operating limits. This would establish where wireless delivery is practical.

uncertain: How much electricity would a complete installation consume for the useful power it delivers?
How would weather, beam spreading, receiver size and exposure limits constrain dependable service?
What output, distance, duration and permitted interruptions would count as success for each intended use?

page.title: Airborne optical power relay networks
page.definition: An airborne network redirects laser light from a ground transmitter to a ground receiver, where photovoltaic cells convert the light to electricity. Its relay aircraft correct beam distortion and divert part of the beam to supply onboard electrical power.

goal.need: Fuel delivery sets the logistics problem addressed by power beaming. On 2 May 2023, the U.S. Army reported a Department of Defense requirement of 4.6 billion gallons of fuel annually. DARPA set an airborne-relay goal to connect energy sources with remote users and supply aircraft without tying their capabilities to carried fuel.

statements.quote: We need ways to deliver energy that overcome the vulnerabilities and other shortcomings of our current paradigm
statements.context: POWER programme manager Paul Jaffe, announcing relay-development teams on 7 September 2023.

statements.quote: Wireless power beaming reduces the need for troops to carry additional fuel and batteries
statements.context: Statement accompanying a U.S. Army contract announcement on 14 November 2024.

completion.title: Three airborne relays deliver 5 kW of electricity between ground sites 200 km apart.
completion.criterion: A 50 kW source laser delivers 10 kW of optical power through three airborne relays to a ground receiver 200 km from the source, yielding 5 kW electrical output. Each relay simultaneously harvests at least 1 kW electrically. The 2022 design constraints require apertures below 1 m diameter, compatibility with existing airframes and compatibility with operations at 60,000 ft or higher.
completion.set_by: DARPA, POWER announcement HR001123S0004, section I.C, with electrical-output metrics retained in Table 1 of DARPA-PS-25-17.
completion.threshold_quote: 200 km transmission range (measured between ground sites)
completion.basis: This entry adopts DARPA’s architecture-specific airborne optical-network target, combining ground delivery and relay power harvesting. DARPA reported over 800 W across 8.6 km for 30 seconds on 16 May 2025, using a ground-to-ground link, in a release that was not peer reviewed. DARPA’s programme page now labels POWER complete.

milestones.title: Optical relay components demonstrate beam redirection, correction and energy harvesting in laboratory tests.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate component technologies for beam redirection, wavefront correction, energy harvesting, laser safety and pointing accuracy in laboratory or subscale tests. DARPA’s 4 June 2025 solicitation reports component prototypes and existence proofs from Phase 1 in an agency account that was not peer reviewed.
milestones.set_by: DARPA, HR001123S0004, Phase 1 risk-reduction activities, pages 8–9.
milestones.threshold_quote: laboratory or subscale demonstrations of novel approaches

milestones.title: One laboratory relay redirects, corrects and harvests a single laser beam as an integrated system.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate all three relay functions together with one laser beam in a laboratory system, with successful completion confirmed by DARPA.
milestones.threshold_quote: lab-scale integrated demonstration of redirection, correction, and harvesting with a single laser beam

milestones.title: One airborne relay above 1.5 km delivers over 3 kW optically to a ground receiver.
milestones.criterion: Meet POWER Phase 2 metrics at White Sands Missile Range with one relay above 1.5 km, over 3 kW delivered optically, over 600 W optically picked off and a receiver aperture above 10 cm and below 20 cm. Accept at least 5 kW at a slant angle from zenith no greater than 45°, use active pointing, tracking and atmospheric correction, and demonstrate adjustable beam pickoff from 0% to 20%. Measure and dissipate the picked-off energy.
milestones.set_by: DARPA, DARPA-PS-25-17, section 3.1 and Table 1. The numerical pass metrics are presented together only in Table 1.

not_found: A public result meeting the integrated laboratory, Phase 2 airborne or Phase 3 network tests was not located.
A technology-wide service threshold specifying wireless power delivery cost, availability and operating duration was not located in programme documents and roadmap searches.
The opened DARPA receiver report supplies neither wall-plug efficiency at 8.6 km nor the number and dates of individual test runs.
The Naval Research Laboratory’s power-beaming report dated 17 June 2026 could not be opened.
